newsitem.title: CHINA: First official U.S. cherry shipment lands in China.
newsitem.headline: First official U.S. cherry shipment lands in China.

text.p: The first official shipment of Washington cherries to China since the 1995 signing of a trade agreement has arrived in Shanghai, but the high price is likely to keep them off Chinese tables for now.
The cherries arrived in China's biggest city by courier flight late Thursday in time for a Friday promotion organised by the U.S. Agricultural Trade Office, Shanghai director Scott Reynolds said.
But at a cost and freight price of $50-$60 per 20-pound case, the cherries would retail in Shanghai at 70-80 yuan ($8.40-$9.60) per pound, he said.

"This is the first year, so we don't expect to sell huge amounts in the Chinese market straight away," said Reynolds, adding that some Chinese importers had expressed interest but had not made any orders for the fruit.
The cherries would cost about $1.50-$2.00 a pound in the United States but were subject to a 48-percent import tariff in China and a value-added tax, U.S. officials said.

The signing of the protocol in 1995 under which China agreed to import Washington cherries was considered a breakthrough at the time and came after exhaustive food safety talks focusing on plant safety issues.
It was the result of a March 1995 pact between Beijing and Washington in which China agreed to protect U.S. copyrights and base its food safety standards of plant and animal imports on sound science.

In return, Washington agreed to support China's entry into the World Trade Organisation. U.S. officials said Friday they hoped the tariffs on the cherries would be dealt with as part of China's WTO membership application.
They said that while this is the first official shipment, Washington cherries had already entered China, most likely through the porous southern ports via Hong Kong.
